rules.when: The task depends on fresh news, current events, live public facts, or recent market and product changes.
rules.why: Grok is the preferred dispatch when current web-connected context is central to the work. grok has one provider family, so it needs no provider declaration.

rules.when: The task is a trivial mechanical edit such as a rote rename, formatting sweep, targeted typo fix, or simple file gathering.
rules.why: Use the cheapest fast profile when the task is narrow and low ambiguity. The session default model is the right default for code work, and a stronger model earns its cost only when the task really needs one.

rules.when: The task is code work a third-party model service would read, and the operator accepts that service's current data-retention terms.
rules.why: opencode is multi-provider, so typed resolution needs its provider named. It has no effort axis, so an effort here is a CREW_DISPATCH error rather than a stronger run. Confirm the model in the live `opencode models` catalog before dispatch.

rules.when: The task is a big or ambiguous multi-file feature, a risky refactor, or work that requires holding many moving parts in mind.
rules.why: Use a strong coding profile for big, ambiguous work; resolve the alternatives through quota-array-dispatch. The rule floor is the captain's own headroom policy: a known shortfall falls through to default, while a floor naming a provider or scope quota-axi does not report is unverifiable and escalates instead. A profile floor guards one candidate and always reads that profile's own provider.
